answer:
Your objection deserves a straight answer, and here it is: the case for Jesus's divinity doesn't hang on John alone, and it doesn't rest on "I am God" being spoken as a bare formula anywhere. Even granting Mark and Matthew's different emphases, the earliest layer of Christian confession is already staggeringly high. Paul—writing in the 50s, earlier than any Gospel—quotes what looks like a pre-existing hymn declaring that at Jesus's name "every knee should bow" (Philippians 2:10), language Isaiah applied to YHWH alone (Isaiah 45:23). That's not sixty years of legendary accretion; that's a confession already in circulation within two decades of the crucifixion, among Jews who inherited the Shema's ferocious monotheism (Deuteronomy 6:4) and knew exactly what it cost to give worship to anyone but God (Exodus 20:3-5).

So the real question isn't "did John invent this" but "why did Jewish monotheists, allergic to idolatry, begin applying Israel's own God-language to a crucified man within a generation of his death?" John's Gospel makes explicit what the earliest hymns and titles already imply—but he didn't invent the phenomenon of Jesus receiving worship without rebuking it. Thomas's confession, "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28), is the Gospel's climax, not its premise—and Jesus's acceptance of it, with a blessing on those who'll believe without seeing, shows the author presenting this as the verdict the evidence itself compels, not a late theological add-on grafted onto silence.

I'd also gently push back on treating Mark and Matthew as devoid of the claim—they contain the Son of Man enthroned with the Ancient of Days, divine prerogatives like forgiving sins, and titles reserved for God. The trajectory isn't invention; it's the earliest strands converging on what John states plainly.

transcript.content: Look, I'll grant you that the explicit "I am God" statement doesn't appear in Mark or Matthew—the two earliest Gospels we have. What we *do* see in those accounts is Jesus speaking about the kingdom of God, calling people to repentance, and using a lot of parabolic language. But the "I am God" sayings? They're concentrated almost entirely in John, written 60–70 years after the crucifixion by an author we don't even know. That looks to me like theological development, not eyewitness memory—the kind of thing that happens when a teacher gets deified over time by communities who need him to be more than human. So where's the evidence that Jesus *himself* actually claimed divinity, rather than that claim being something his followers invented about him?
